newsitem.title: FRANCE: Legal experts urge reform to fend off French gloom.
newsitem.headline: Legal experts urge reform to fend off French gloom.

text.p: Five top legal experts called on Tuesday for constitutional and political reforms to avert a possible crisis and correct what they said were basic flaws in French democracy fuelling the country's current gloomy mood.

They urged cutting the presidential term to five years from seven, making it easier to call a referendum, boosting local power, giving the opposition a bigger role and banning politicians from simultaneously holding various elective offices.
Their suggestions, prominently published in the influential daily Le Monde, coincided with the campaign for a parliamentary election on May 25-June 1.
The five, including top constitutional expert Georges Vedel, noted that voters had always returned the ruling party to power in the first 15 years of the 39-year-old Fifth Republic.
But they always voted it down in the past 15 years.

"Glorious growth during the 1960s and the desperation of unemployment in the 1980s and 1990s do not explain everything. France's gloom is not only social but also moral and institutional," they wrote.
They said France, where professional politicians monopolised power, was ridden by sleaze scandals.
Abstention, especially among young people, was growing with each election and the country was, with Austria, the only one in Europe where the far-right polled well above 10 percent.

Noting that major constitutional reforms in France had always emerged following a crisis -- the 1870 war against Germany, World War Two and the Algerian war of independence produced the Third, Fourth and Fifth Republics -- they called for changes before a fresh disaster produces the Sixth Republic.
"We believe that precise, deliberate and simultaneous reforms could produce or lead to necessary and urgent changes," they said.

The experts said the seven-year presidential term was the longest in Europe, and cutting it to the same five-year duration as the National Assembly's term would restore harmony in the democratic cycle.
Conservative President Jacques Chirac and the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand both backed a shorter presidential term only to quietly drop the suggestion once in power.
In order to boost democracy, the experts suggested the president should share his right to call a referendum with parliamentarians provided they get the support of a significant number of citizens.

They said French politicians had become Europe's laughing stock for being allowed to hold several elected mandates, both national and local. They suggested allowing only one mandate and banning cabinet ministers from holding any other job.

In order to end sleaze scandals and stifling domination of the state by the ruling party, they proposed drastically cutting the number of public jobs alloted by the government and giving the opposition a bigger role in state watchdogs.

"The ability to hold several offices is turning us into a laughing stock, but corruption, the rulers' all-powerfulness, their idea that they own power, their contempt for control...are no laughing matter," one of the experts, university professor Yves Meny, said.
